content: The youngest and sickest patients, as well as those who demonstrate adherence to treatment and can be monitored for adverse events, should be prioritized for care. However, patients facing socioeconomic barriers to adherence or those living in remote, rural, or underserved communities with limited access to technical resources for treatment monitoring may be disproportionately disadvantaged. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) emphasized that injectable-free treatment regimens are easier to decentralize and could help reduce health inequities in such settings without compromising outcomes across specific populations. Additionally, the GDG noted that the absence of audiometry requirements in these regimens simplifies monitoring, even though electrocardiography (ECG) is necessary for bedaquiline-containing regimens. However, the group stressed that ECG monitoring should not be a differentiating factor between regimens, as patients receiving injectable agents like amikacin also require regular cardiac monitoring. While it is acknowledged that not all patients in certain settings may have access to ECG monitoring, the increasing availability of ECG at peripheral levels could improve equity. Cost-effectiveness modeling conducted in South Africa demonstrated that a 9–12-month all-oral regimen is both cost-saving and more effective than shorter regimens containing injectable agents under most modeled conditions. The projected cost savings average approximately $1,000 per patient, primarily due to reduced costs associated with injectable delivery and management of recurrent or secondary cases. Even in scenarios where the all-oral regimen is not cost-saving due to higher drug prices, it remains cost-effective, with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of $400 per disability-adjusted life year averted. From a health equity perspective, the GDG concluded that the all-oral regimen could increase equity by being more accessible to disadvantaged populations. A qualitative study involving patients and civil society representatives revealed that most patients prioritize regimens with fewer and less severe side effects, even if the treatment duration is longer. Survivors of drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) expressed a willingness to accept longer treatments with fewer adverse effects over shorter regimens with more severe side effects. However, some participants preferred shorter regimens to return to normal life more quickly, even if associated with higher risks. The GDG recommended a shorter, all-oral, bedaquiline-containing regimen of 9–12 months for eligible patients with confirmed multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) who have not been exposed to second-line TB medicines in this regimen for more than one month and in whom fluoroquinolone resistance has been excluded. This recommendation is conditional due to very low certainty in the evidence, primarily based on observational data from South Africa. The group noted that the regimen showed a better success-to-unfavorable outcome ratio and reduced loss to follow-up compared to other regimens. Implementation of this regimen requires careful patient selection, rapid and accurate drug-susceptibility testing (DST), and monitoring for bedaquiline resistance. Laboratory infrastructure must be strengthened to support genotypic and phenotypic testing for companion drugs in the regimen. The removal of injectable agents offers significant advantages, including reduced pain and adverse events for patients and greater convenience for healthcare workers. However, successful implementation also depends on sustainable systems changes, uninterrupted drug supply, and active drug safety monitoring. The GDG highlighted the need for further research to address gaps in evidence, including studies comparing all-oral shorter regimens with and without linezolid, assessments of these regimens in special populations (e.g., pregnant women, children), and mechanisms of resistance acquisition to bedaquiline. Efforts to standardize data collection globally are also necessary to inform future recommendations. In conclusion, the GDG strongly supports the use of a shorter, all-oral, bedaquiline-containing regimen for MDR/RR-TB patients, recognizing its potential to improve outcomes, reduce costs, and promote health equity.
